name: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
title: The Threshold of Machine Authorship
answer: The threshold of machine authorship is the line between a human creator and a generative system that produces text, images, code, or music. It asks who, if anyone, can claim copyright in output that a model generated from a prompt, and whether selection, arrangement, or editing by a person is enough to cross that line. The question also reaches patent inventorship, where many patent systems require a natural person to be named as inventor. The site tracks 147 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows how quickly this boundary is being tested.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The threshold is not a single technology but a set of records and processes: model training data, prompt logs, version histories, output files, and human edit trails. Registries, courts, and rights holders rely on metadata, timestamps, and terms of service to reconstruct who contributed what. Generative tools often produce output without clear provenance, so the infrastructure of authorship is really an evidence chain. In practice, that chain may include model cards, dataset documentation, and audit logs.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners compare the human contribution against the machine contribution, looking for creative choices in prompts, revisions, curation, and arrangement. They review contracts, platform terms, and disclosure requirements to see what rights the user or the provider claims. They also map the output against existing works to assess infringement risk and originality. The analysis is fact specific, so two similar prompts can lead to different authorship conclusions depending on the human role.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are unclear ownership, infringement claims, and false claims of authorship. Provenance matters because a registry or court may ask for the source of training data, the model version, and the human steps that shaped the output. Disclosure rules and registration practices are emerging, and they vary by jurisdiction and by whether the work is literary, visual, or functional. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages and 6940 state AI bills reflect how fragmented the rules remain.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: More guidance is likely from copyright offices and courts on how much human control is enough, along with more disclosure requirements for generative outputs. Patent offices may continue to reject machine-only inventorship while allowing human inventors who use AI as a tool. Standards for provenance, watermarking, and content credentials are likely to become part of the authorship record. The volume of active litigation, 147 cases with 92 on intellectual property, suggests the threshold will be defined case by case for some time.
